articleTitle: Recent developments in glass insulators
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: It may be considered remarkable that such a brittle substance as glass can be used for general purpose insulators subjected to heavy mechanieal and electrical shock. Developments over the last few years, however, have resulted in so great an improvement in technical procedure that a glass insulator can now be obtained which seems able to compare very favourably both in cost and performance with the best porcelain products. The following remarks show in a general way something of the method of manufacture and performance of these glass insulators.

publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: As mentioned in the paper, the Anglo American Group has employed earth leakage protection since 1932, and the results obtained have justified the small additional cost involved in installing the necessary equipment. Since the earth fault current is limited, the damage resulting from this relatively small current, which usually precedes a phase short circuit, is also limited, and enables the circuit to be isolated before the short circuit condition obtains, or, at least, reduces its time of duration.

articleTitle: Electricity in medicine
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Mr. President, Ladies and Gentlemen: At the outset, permit me to thank your Association for having asked me to address you to-night at this joint meeting of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers and the University of the Witwatersrand. It would, however, be taking advantage of the great honour you have done me, if I did not immediately disclaim any pretensions to a knowledge of electricity. My object to-night is to draw attention to that very limited knowledge on the part of the medical practitioner, and to the even more limited use of electricity as a means for determining the condition of the patient and for the alleviation of the sick.

articleTitle: Factors influencing electric power transmission on the reef
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The first three power stations of the Victoria Falls and Transvaal Power Company, Limited, were located on the Reef, at Brakpan, Simmerpan and Eosherville. These stations were adjacent to the load centres and long distance transmission lines were not necessary for conveying the power* from the stations to the various load points. In the early days, the distribution network on the Reef consisted of 10 kV and 20 kV overhead lines and, at a later### date, 40 kV distribution feeders and interconncctors were adopted. “With the growth of load and the general extension of the system, it became necessary to construct further power stations and, for reasons not relevant to the subject matter of this paper, these stations were located some distance from the Reef; the first of these was Vereeniging, 35 miles to the south of Johannesburg, followed by Witbank, 64 miles north-east of Brakpan and, later, Klip was installed, this station being about 32 miles to the south of Johannesburg.

articleTitle: Examiners resume of thesis entitled “the application of direct current to small municipal electricity supply undertakings”
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: There is no novelty in the use of direct current for municipal electricity supply, but the general opinion seems to be that this is an obsolete system, best relegated to oblivion. The engineers of many undertakings that have changed over from direct current to alternating current speak bitterly of their early experience with D.C., and regard with amazement the survival of certain direct current schemes in this country. The only reasons that occur to them to account for such survivals are conservatism, unwillingness or inability to scrap obsolete equipment, and lack of funds to effect a change over.

articleTitle: The history of the institution of electrical engineers (1871-1931)
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Engineers are generally thought to be practical beings. They make things work, construct out of the raw materials those machines used, we hope, for the advancement of our civilisation. Because of this they arc often regarded as living hut for the present, lacking in an imagination of the future and devoid of any feelings of awe or reverence for the great pioneers of the past. Nothing could be further from the truth. Perhaps more than any other professional class, the engineer must possess imagination, he must “dream dreams and see visions,” he must be able to conceive in his mind's eye the finished product before any work has been started on it and he must then proceed determinedly forward until the figment of his imagination takes on its true form. As to the past., the engineer knows full well that the common knowledge of to-day has only been given to us by the industrious endeavour of those of yesterday who attacked the problems which confronted them. He realises, too, what useful lessons may be learnt from those who laid the foundations of the profession — lessons which can be of considerable aid in meeting the difficulties encountered in present times.

articleTitle: Valedictory address
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: May I be permitted to preface my Valedictory Address with the remark that while the presentation of such an address has been established by custom it seems to me to be inherently incorrect. I presume that initially it was intended to cover a review of the year's activities, but this is now very admirably done in the Annual Report and there is little left for the retiring President to say on that score. Like my predecessors in office, I find the period of stock-taking somewhat painful, largely because of the sins of omission on my part. At the same time one is wholeheartedly grateful for the support which has been so ungrudgingly given by the Vice-Presidents and Members of Council, particularly as residence outside the Witwatersrand and clash of engagements has compelled me to call upon good-hearted members to deputise for me on several occasions. To all I express my profound thanks.

articleTitle: An investigation of the burning of conductors on overhead lines
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: When suggesting to Professor Randall the investigation undertaken by the authors one could foresee ninny obstacles in the way of obtaining quantitative results, but one hoped that as a result of the investigation one would obtain some useful information in regard to the manner in which conductors become burnt or damaged as a result of arcing. The authors are to be congratulated on the thorough manner in which they tackled the investigation. It is unfortunate that owing to insufficient time and power they were not in a position to push their investigation sufficiently far for the results to be of general use in solving the problem as to the maximum arcing time allowable on overhead conductors without serious damage being done to these.

articleTitle: Presidential Address
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Before starting on the main subject of this Address I should like once again to thank you for electing me as President of our Institute for the coming year. The Institute, with its large and varied membership, totalling now to the imposing figure of 819, as given in our last year's Report, has gradually over the years grown from strength to strength, until to-day it is accepted as being one of the principal bodies of technical opinion in this country. To be elected President of the Institute is, therefore, an honour which I shall certainly value highly for the rest of my life.

articleTitle: “Neutral earthing and earth leakage protection”
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Mr. J. G. Wellings (Visitor): That portion of the paper dealing with earth leakage protection reveals the great importance which attaches to the proper co-ordination of current transformer and relay characteristics if satisfactory performance is to he obtained. There still seems to be in the minds of many users the idea that satisfactory performance of protective gear can be obtained by specifying the current transformers and relay separately, and in many instances purchasing them from separate sources according to which seems to be the best article available. While no doubt this may result in excellent current transformers and relays being obtained as such, the combination of these components forms a protective gear system and may prove very far from perfect. In my opinion, which is supported by very exhaustive testing on protective gear systems as a whole and extensive experience with same in the field, purchasers should specify only the requirements of the protective gear as as a whole, and leave to the manufacturers the responsibility of supplying suitable transformers and relays, the combination of which should he tested to show compliance with the protective gear requirements in the same as any other piece of apparatus is tested to show that it conforms with its guarantee.

articleTitle: Report on an investigation into the electrical properties of concrete
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The electrical properties of concrete have as yet not been extensively investigated. A Frenchman, P. Perrier, did some important work in this direction which lead to the publication of two papers. In one of these entitled “A New Industrial Insulator.” he describes tests performed on a special concrete, which exhibited good insulating properties.### Mr. E. Lambert was responsible for evolving this new type of concrete. In Mr. Ferrier's other paper, the application of concrete as an insulator in high voltage circuits is discussed. These tests were conducted in France over a period of several years and the effect of the different weather conditions on the concrete was examined.
